nameStory: The red-belted bumble bee gets its name from the distinctive reddish band of hairs that wraps around its fuzzy abdomen like a colorful belt. This rusty-red "belt" stands out beautifully against the bee's black body, making it one of the more distinctively marked bumble bees you'll encounter in New England gardens and woodlands.
description: The red-belted bumble bee is a small, stocky bumble bee with a fuzzy black body decorated with bright yellow and distinctive reddish-orange hair patches. Queens are the largest at about 2/3 of an inch long, while workers and males are smaller at around half an inch. Like all bumble bees, they're robust and fuzzy with a gentle buzzing flight pattern, but this species is noticeably smaller than many of their bumble bee cousins.

idTips.label: Red abdominal band
idTips.description: Look for the telltale reddish-orange belt of soft hairs wrapping around the middle sections of the abdomen - this rusty band contrasts sharply with the black body and bright yellow patches

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than most other bumble bees - queens are only about 2/3 inch long, roughly the size of your thumbnail, with a compact, rounded build

idTips.label: Yellow head markings
idTips.description: The fuzzy head has scattered gray and yellowish hairs mixed with black, giving it a salt-and-pepper appearance when viewed up close

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: The red belt can sometimes appear more orange or even be replaced by black hairs in some individuals, while yellow markings may vary in intensity

idTips.label: Dense, soft fur
idTips.description: The entire body is covered in exceptionally soft, dense hairs that look almost plush - like a tiny flying teddy bear with bright racing stripes

habitat: Red-belted bumble bees prefer wooded areas and forest edges throughout New England, but readily adapt to urban parks, suburban gardens, and any area with abundant flowers. They're particularly drawn to areas where woods meet open spaces, such as hiking trail edges, woodland clearings, and backyard gardens near tree lines.

seasonality.spring: Queens emerge from winter hibernation and can be seen visiting early flowers like wild strawberry blossoms and spring wildflowers as they search for nesting sites.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when workers are most visible, busily visiting garden flowers, goldenrod, clovers, and sunflowers throughout the day with their characteristic gentle buzzing.
seasonality.fall: New queens and males emerge for mating flights, often seen on late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod before queens seek winter shelter.
seasonality.winter: Only mated queens survive, hibernating underground or in protected spaces like hollow logs until spring warmth awakens them.

funFact: Red-belted bumble bees are like nature's living mood rings - the same species can have completely different color patterns due to genetic switches that turn their red belt black or their yellow patches dark, creating natural disguises that even fooled scientists for years!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with brown-belted bumble bees, but red-belted bees have a distinctly rusty-red or orange band while brown-belted bees have a more brownish band. Memory trick: "Red-belted = Rusty-red, Brown-belted = Brownish."
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called the "red-banded bumble bee" in older field guides, and the scientific name "rufocinctus" literally means "red-belted" in Latin. Despite being called "short-tongued," they can still reach nectar in many garden flowers that longer-tongued bees prefer.
compareHints: Red-belted bumble bees are much smaller than common eastern bumble bees and lack the solid yellow thorax of many other species. Unlike the tricolored bumble bee which has distinct bands of yellow, black, and orange in neat stripes, red-belted bees have their colors more mixed together with the red band being the standout feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bumble bees, the Common Eastern Bumble Bee is distinguished by its predominantly black coloration with limited yellow banding, unlike the Brown-belted Bumble Bee which has brown fur, or the Tricolored Bumble Bee which sports distinctive white patches.
Among New England's bumble bees, the Brown-belted is most similar to the Red-belted Bumble Bee, but has a duller, more brownish belt versus bright rusty-red.
Among New England's many bumble bee species, the Two-spotted stands out for its clean black and yellow pattern with those diagnostic two spots.
The orange band is what sets the Tricolored Bumble Bee apart from its many relatives in New England.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, the Perplexing Bumble Bee has more white hairs on the head and distinctive reddish mandible tips.
Unlike the Common Eastern Bumble Bee which has more irregular yellow patches, the Yellow-banded has clean, complete yellow bands.

Northern Amber Bumble Bees stand out from other New England bumble bees by their uniform golden-yellow body combined with contrasting pale head hairs—most other species have distinct color bands or patterns.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, Half-black Bumble Bees are noticeably smaller and have more defined black banding rather than the Common Eastern's more blended yellow and black pattern.

Among New England's bumble bees, the Golden Northern stands out for its uniform golden-yellow coloration, while most relatives like the Common Eastern Bumble Bee have distinct black and white/yellow banding patterns.
Unlike social bumble bees in its genus, the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee lacks pollen baskets (specialized hairs for carrying pollen) since it doesn't need to provision its own nest.
Unlike other cuckoo bumble bees in New England like the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee, the Yellowish Cuckoo has more muted, golden-yellow tones rather than bright lemon-yellow.
